questions.question: “Lay-off” under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 refers to the failure, refusal or inability of an employer to give employment to a workman whose name is on the muster rolls and who has not been retrenched, on account of:

options.label: A
options.text: misconduct proved against the workman after inquiry

options.label: B
options.text: the workman attaining the age of superannuation

options.label: C
options.text: shortage of coal, power or raw materials, accumulation of stocks, breakdown of machinery, natural calamity or similar reason

options.label: D
options.text: voluntary abandonment of service by the workman

rectification.principle: Section 2(kkk) defines lay-off as temporary inability to employ a muster-roll workman due to shortage of coal, power, raw materials, stock accumulation, machinery breakdown, or natural calamity.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing lay-off with disciplinary dismissal or superannuation.
rectification.howToRectify: Lay-off = temporary operational/resource inability while workman stays on muster rolls.

questions.subject: Labour & Industrial Law
questions.question: Under Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, before a workman who has been in continuous service for not less than one year is validly retrenched, the employer must, among other conditions:

options.label: A
options.text: obtain the written consent of every other workman in the establishment

options.label: B
options.text: give the workman one month’s notice (or wages in lieu) and pay compensation at fifteen days’ average pay for every completed year of continuous service

options.label: C
options.text: pay compensation equal to three years’ wages in all cases

options.label: D
options.text: secure the prior approval of the trade union in writing

rectification.principle: Section 25F requires one month's notice (or wages in lieu) plus retrenchment compensation at 15 days' average pay per completed year of continuous service.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Forgetting the exact 1 month + 15 days/year statutory formula.
rectification.howToRectify: s.25F = 1 month's notice/pay + 15 days' average pay × completed years.

questions.subject: Labour & Industrial Law
questions.question: A strike is commenced by workmen in a public utility service without giving the notice required by Section 22 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Such a strike is:

options.label: A
options.text: legal, since the right to strike is absolute

options.label: B
options.text: legal only if a majority of workmen participate

options.label: C
options.text: illegal, being in contravention of the notice requirements applicable to public utility services

options.label: D
options.text: neither legal nor illegal, but merely irregular

rectification.principle: Under Section 24 read with Section 22 ID Act, a strike in a public utility service commenced without mandatory prior notice is illegal.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming majority support makes an unnotified public utility strike lawful.
rectification.howToRectify: Public utility service + no s.22 notice = illegal strike (s.24).

questions.subject: Labour & Industrial Law
questions.question: Closure of an undertaking under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 differs from lay-off and retrenchment principally in that closure means:

options.label: A
options.text: a temporary stoppage of work with the intention to resume

options.label: B
options.text: termination of an individual workman for reasons other than punishment

options.label: C
options.text: refusal to employ a workman on the muster rolls for a temporary period

options.label: D
options.text: the permanent closing down of a place of employment or part thereof

rectification.principle: Section 2(cc) defines 'closure' as the permanent closing down of a place of employment or part thereof.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing closure with temporary lay-off or individual retrenchment.
rectification.howToRectify: Closure = permanent shutdown of the place of employment.

questions.subject: Labour & Industrial Law
questions.question: Engaging workmen as “badlis”, casuals or temporaries and continuing them as such for years with the object of depriving them of the status and privileges of permanent workmen is, under the Fifth Schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, an example of:

options.label: A
options.text: an unfair labour practice on the part of the employer

options.label: B
options.text: a lawful managerial prerogative

options.label: C
options.text: a legitimate lockout

options.label: D
options.text: a protected strike by workmen

rectification.principle: The Fifth Schedule (read with ss.2(ra) and 25T) classifies continuing casual/badli/temporary workers for years to deny permanent status as an unfair labour practice by the employer.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Viewing prolonged temporary engagement as an unrestricted management right.
rectification.howToRectify: Perpetual temporary status to avoid permanency = Fifth Schedule unfair labour practice.

questions.subject: Consumer Protection Act
questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a “product liability” action enables a complainant to claim compensation from a product manufacturer, product seller or product service provider for harm caused by:

options.label: A
options.text: a defective product or deficient service, including manufacturing, design or warning defects

options.label: B
options.text: any commercial loss suffered in a purely business-to-business transaction

options.label: C
options.text: delay in delivery alone, irrespective of any defect or harm

options.label: D
options.text: breach of an arbitration clause in the sale contract

rectification.principle: Sections 82–87 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 allow product liability claims for harm caused by defective products (manufacturing, design, or warning defects) or deficient services.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Forgetting that commercial B2B transactions fall outside consumer protection.
rectification.howToRectify: Product liability = harm caused by defective product or deficient service.

questions.subject: Consumer Protection Act
questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 made under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, an e-commerce entity is, among other duties, required to:

options.label: A
options.text: refuse to entertain any consumer complaint about goods sold on its platform

options.label: B
options.text: appoint a grievance officer and display details enabling consumers to make complaints, while not adopting unfair trade practices

options.label: C
options.text: charge cancellation fees on consumers without disclosing them, as it sees fit

options.label: D
options.text: escape all liability by describing itself merely as an intermediary in every case

rectification.principle: The E-Commerce Rules, 2020 oblige e-commerce entities to appoint a grievance officer, display complaint redressal contact details, and abstain from unfair trade practices.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming intermediary status creates blanket exemption from consumer duties.
rectification.howToRectify: E-commerce duties = grievance officer + complaint transparency + no unfair trade practices.

questions.subject: Consumer Protection Act
questions.question: Under Section 2(46) read with Section 49 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a term of a contract which causes a significant change in the rights of the consumer, such as requiring excessive security deposits or imposing a disproportionate penalty for breach, may be declared by the appropriate forum to be:

options.label: A
options.text: a valid and binding term immune from review

options.label: B
options.text: a mere unfair trade practice attracting no remedy

options.label: C
options.text: an “unfair contract” term, which the State Commission or National Commission may declare null and void

options.label: D
options.text: enforceable only against the trader and not the consumer

rectification.principle: Section 2(46) defines 'unfair contract' and Sections 49 & 59 empower the State Commission and National Commission to declare unfair contract terms null and void.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Missing the new 2019 statutory power given to State and National Commissions over unfair contracts.
rectification.howToRectify: s.2(46) + s.49/59 = Commissions can strike down 'unfair contract' terms as null and void.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.question: A maintains a maintenance claim for his minor child born of a void marriage. The correct legal position regarding such a child’s right to maintenance from the father is that:

options.label: A
options.text: the child has no right to maintenance because the marriage is void

options.label: B
options.text: maintenance is payable only until the child attains five years of age

options.label: C
options.text: the obligation to maintain falls solely on the mother in every case

options.label: D
options.text: the child, being deemed legitimate under Section 16 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, is entitled to maintenance from the father

rectification.principle: A child born of a void marriage is deemed legitimate under s.16 HMA and is entitled to maintenance from the father under s.20 HAMA and s.125 CrPC.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Denying maintenance because the parents' marriage is void.
rectification.howToRectify: Void marriage -> child deemed legitimate (s.16 HMA) -> entitled to father's maintenance.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.statuteRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Parts I & II)
questions.question: Two Indian companies refer their dispute to an arbitration seated in Singapore. After the foreign award is rendered, one party seeks to challenge it in an Indian court under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Which Part of the Act governs an arbitration seated outside India, and what is the consequence for such a challenge?

options.label: A
options.text: Part I applies in full, so the Section 34 setting-aside remedy is freely available

options.label: B
options.text: Part II governs enforcement of foreign awards, and Section 34 of Part I does not apply to set aside an award made at a foreign seat

options.label: C
options.text: The award is automatically void because two Indian parties cannot choose a foreign seat

options.label: D
options.text: Both Parts apply simultaneously, giving the party a double remedy

rectification.principle: Per BALCO (2012), Part I (including s.34 setting aside) does not apply to foreign-seated arbitrations; Part II governs enforcement of foreign awards in India.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Applying the overruled Bhatia International view or doubting Indian parties' freedom to pick a foreign seat.
rectification.howToRectify: Foreign seat -> Part II governs enforcement; s.34 setting aside unavailable.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A contract names “the seat of arbitration shall be London” while hearings for convenience are conducted in New Delhi. A party argues that Indian courts have supervisory jurisdiction because the hearings took place in India. Following the distinction between “seat” and “venue”, the correct position is:

options.label: A
options.text: The venue of hearings always determines the curial law and supervisory jurisdiction

options.label: B
options.text: Indian courts have full supervisory jurisdiction whenever any hearing occurs in India

options.label: C
options.text: The chosen seat (London) fixes the supervisory jurisdiction and curial law; the New Delhi venue is merely a convenient geographical location for hearings

options.label: D
options.text: The parties cannot fix any seat once hearings have begun elsewhere

rectification.principle: The arbitral 'seat' (London) determines supervisory court jurisdiction and curial law; 'venue' (New Delhi) is merely a convenient location for hearings (BALCO; BGS SGS Soma).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Conflating hearing location (venue) with juridical seat.
rectification.howToRectify: Seat = jurisdiction & curial law; Venue = hearing location.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: A party seeks to enforce in India a commercial arbitral award made in a country that is a signatory to the New York Convention and which the Central Government has notified as a reciprocating territory. Enforcement of such a foreign award is governed by which provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996?

options.label: A
options.text: Sections 53 to 60, dealing with Geneva Convention awards

options.label: B
options.text: Section 36, on enforcement of purely domestic awards

options.label: C
options.text: Sections 34 and 37, on setting aside and appeals

options.label: D
options.text: Sections 44 to 49 of Part II, Chapter I, which give effect to the New York Convention

rectification.principle: Sections 44 to 49 (Part II, Chapter I) govern enforcement of New York Convention awards in India, whereas Sections 53 to 60 govern Geneva Convention awards.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Swapping New York Convention (ss.44–49) with Geneva Convention (ss.53–60).
rectification.howToRectify: New York Convention = ss.44–49; Geneva Convention = ss.53–60.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Resisting enforcement of a New York Convention foreign award in India, the award-debtor pleads that enforcement would be contrary to the “public policy of India”. On the scope of the public-policy ground for refusing enforcement of a foreign award under Section 48 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the correct position is:

options.label: A
options.text: The ground is construed narrowly and does not permit a review on the merits; “patent illegality” is not a ground for refusing a foreign award

options.label: B
options.text: Any error of law on the face of the award justifies refusal of enforcement

options.label: C
options.text: The enforcing court must re-hear the entire dispute afresh on the evidence

options.label: D
options.text: Public policy here is identical to and as wide as the domestic patent-illegality ground

rectification.principle: Under Section 48 (Shri Lal Mahal v. Progetto Grano), public policy for foreign awards is construed narrowly without merits review, and 'patent illegality' applies only to domestic awards (s.34(2A)).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Applying domestic 'patent illegality' to foreign-award enforcement.
rectification.howToRectify: Foreign awards (s.48): narrow public policy, NO merits review, NO patent illegality.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Before a foreign-seated arbitration has commenced, an Indian party fears that assets located in India will be dissipated and seeks urgent interim protection from an Indian court. Which provision of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 permits a court to grant interim measures in support of a foreign-seated arbitration, subject to the parties not having agreed to exclude it?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 17, since only the foreign tribunal can grant any interim relief

options.label: B
options.text: The proviso to Section 2(2), which makes Section 9 (interim measures by court) applicable to international commercial arbitrations even where the seat is outside India, unless the parties agree otherwise

options.label: C
options.text: Section 27, on court assistance in taking evidence only

options.label: D
options.text: No provision; Indian courts can never assist a foreign-seated arbitration

rectification.principle: The proviso to Section 2(2) extends Section 9 (court interim relief) to foreign-seated international commercial arbitrations unless excluded by agreement.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Overlooking the 2015 statutory proviso to s.2(2).
rectification.howToRectify: Proviso to s.2(2) keeps Section 9 interim relief available for foreign-seated arbitrations unless excluded.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: Two parties resolve a commercial dispute through a mediation conducted under the Mediation Act, 2023 and sign a written settlement. As to the legal status and enforceability of such a mediated settlement agreement under that Act, the correct position is:

options.label: A
options.text: It is a mere moral understanding with no enforceable value

options.label: B
options.text: It must first be converted into a civil-court decree before it has any effect at all

options.label: C
options.text: A mediated settlement agreement (other than one arrived at in a court-referred mediation, which is governed otherwise) is final and binding and is enforceable in the same manner as a judgment, decree or order of a court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908

options.label: D
options.text: It can be unilaterally repudiated by either party at any time without consequence

rectification.principle: Under Section 27 of the Mediation Act, 2023, a signed mediated settlement agreement (other than court-referred) is final, binding, and directly enforceable like a court decree under the CPC.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Thinking a separate civil suit or prior decree conversion is mandatory.
rectification.howToRectify: Mediation Act 2023 s.27 = directly enforceable as a CPC decree.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.question: During mediation under the Mediation Act, 2023, one party makes admissions and discloses settlement proposals that ultimately fail. In a later court proceeding the opposing party seeks to lead these in evidence. On the confidentiality of mediation communications, the Act provides that:

options.label: A
options.text: All mediation communications are freely admissible as ordinary evidence

options.label: B
options.text: Confidentiality applies only if the mediator personally objects in writing

options.label: C
options.text: Mediation communications, admissions and proposals are confidential and, as a rule, are not admissible as evidence in any subsequent judicial or arbitral proceeding

options.label: D
options.text: Confidentiality ends the moment the mediation fails to produce a settlement

rectification.principle: Sections 22 and 23 of the Mediation Act, 2023 protect confidentiality of mediation admissions and proposals and bar their admissibility in subsequent judicial or arbitral proceedings.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming confidentiality expires if mediation fails.
rectification.howToRectify: Mediation communications remain confidential and inadmissible even after failed mediation.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & Contempt
questions.question: A practising advocate of standing and ability, whose conduct of cases shows special knowledge in a field of law, is proposed for an elevated status with attendant restrictions, for instance that the advocate shall not appear without a junior or file pleadings on his own. This status and the restrictions flow from which provision of the Advocates Act, 1961?

options.label: A
options.text: Section 16, which provides for the designation of senior advocates by the Supreme Court or a High Court on the basis of ability and standing, with restrictions framed by the Bar Council of India

options.label: B
options.text: Section 30, the right to practise

options.label: C
options.text: Section 24, on persons qualified to be admitted as advocates

options.label: D
options.text: Section 49, the general rule-making power

rectification.principle: Section 16 of the Advocates Act, 1961 governs designation of senior advocates by the Supreme Court or High Courts based on ability and standing, subject to BCI restrictions.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Confusing s.16 with general enrolment (s.24) or right to practise (s.30).
rectification.howToRectify: Senior Advocate designation & restrictions = Section 16 Advocates Act.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & Contempt
questions.question: An advocate sets up a large illuminated hoarding outside the courthouse advertising “Best Divorce Lawyer — Guaranteed Results — Lowest Fees” and circulates pamphlets soliciting clients. Such conduct most directly violates which professional-ethics norm?

options.label: A
options.text: It is perfectly permissible, as advertising is a fundamental right of every advocate

options.label: B
options.text: Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules (Standards of Professional Conduct), which prohibits an advocate from advertising or soliciting work, directly or indirectly

options.label: C
options.text: It is governed solely by the Consumer Protection Act and raises no ethical issue

options.label: D
options.text: It is barred only if the advocate has fewer than ten years at the Bar

rectification.principle: Rule 36 of the BCI Rules forbids advocates from advertising or soliciting work directly or indirectly through hoardings, circulars, or touts.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming commercial advertising is permitted as a fundamental right.
rectification.howToRectify: Rule 36 BCI Rules = strict bar on advocate advertising and solicitation.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & Contempt
questions.question: An indigent accused who cannot afford counsel is being tried for a serious offence. Reflecting both the constitutional guarantee and the advocate’s professional obligation, the duty to render legal aid is best described as:

options.label: A
options.text: A purely optional act of charity that no advocate is expected to perform

options.label: B
options.text: Owed only to clients who can pay a reduced fee

options.label: C
options.text: A duty that arises only after conviction, never during trial

options.label: D
options.text: A duty rooted in the right to free legal aid flowing from Article 39A and Article 21 of the Constitution, reinforced by the advocate’s professional obligation to assist in providing legal aid to the poor

rectification.principle: Free legal aid flows from Article 39A read with Article 21 (Hussainara Khatoon; M.H. Hoskot) and is reinforced by an advocate's BCI ethical obligation to assist the indigent.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Treating legal aid as optional charity rather than a constitutional & ethical duty.
rectification.howToRectify: Free legal aid = Art. 39A + Art. 21 + BCI professional duty.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & Contempt
questions.question: A litigant publishes an article making a factual allegation of corruption against a sitting judge in respect of a decided matter and, when faced with contempt proceedings, pleads that the statement is true and its publication is in the public interest. Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (as amended in 2006), this plea:

options.label: A
options.text: Is never available; truth can never be a defence to contempt

options.label: B
options.text: Automatically results in punishment regardless of any justification

options.label: C
options.text: Is available only if the judge personally consents to the publication

options.label: D
options.text: May be a valid defence under Section 13(b), which permits the court to allow justification by truth as a defence if it is satisfied that it is in the public interest and the request is bona fide

rectification.principle: Inserted in 2006, Section 13(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 permits justification by truth as a valid defence where it is in public interest and the request is bona fide.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Relying on the pre-2006 position where truth was not a statutory defence.
rectification.howToRectify: Post-2006 s.13(b): Truth + Public Interest + Bona Fide = valid defence.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & Contempt
questions.question: A newspaper, in the ordinary course and without any knowledge that a matter was pending, publishes a report that is later said to prejudice that proceeding. On the defence available to such a publisher under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, the correct position is:

options.label: A
options.text: Section 3 provides a defence of innocent publication and distribution where, at the time of publication, the person had no reasonable grounds for believing that the proceeding was pending

options.label: B
options.text: No defence exists; every publication touching a pending matter is automatically contempt

options.label: C
options.text: The publisher escapes only by paying compensation to the affected litigant

options.label: D
options.text: Innocent publication is a defence only for advocates, not for newspapers

rectification.principle: Section 3 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 provides the defence of innocent publication and distribution when the publisher had no reasonable grounds to believe proceedings were pending.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Assuming contempt liability is strict even without knowledge of pending proceedings.
rectification.howToRectify: Section 3 Contempt of Courts Act = innocent publication defence absent knowledge of pendency.
